passage:
Tuesday night.

Today a caller who gave the name Nikita, from my bank's security team, was so friendly. Said my card would be blocked in ten minutes unless I read out the code that had just arrived. I actually had the message open. My thumb was over the digits when I remembered that a bank should never ask for that code.

I said, "Please hold, I'll call the number on the back of my card." The caller's voice went sharp, and then the line went dead. My heart is still racing. I feel silly at how close I came to trusting that warm voice.

Told Amma and my roommate. Amma says anybody can be fooled. I've saved the bank's official number in my phone.

Gautam

qa.q: What name did the caller give?
qa.a: The caller gave the name Nikita, from the bank's security team.

qa.q: Why did Gautam nearly read out the code?
qa.a: The caller was friendly and urgent, saying the card would be blocked in ten minutes, and that mix of warmth and fear almost worked; Gautam even had the message open.

qa.q: What should Gautam do next time a caller says they are from the bank?
qa.a: Never share the code, hang up, and call the official number on the back of the card.

qa.q: How might the caller see Gautam's request to call back?
qa.a: The caller loses the pressure that the trick depends on, which may explain the sharp voice and the sudden hang-up.

grounding: A friendly, urgent caller posing as the bank exploits Gautam's trust and fear; Gautam stops at the last moment and verifies through the official number.

passage: "Usha-didi, I want to tell you what happened last week, so you're careful too. I'm Harish. A man called me, very friendly, very polite. He said he was from my bank's fraud department, that someone was trying to use my card in Delhi, and he needed to block it right now. He knew my name and the last four digits of my card. He sounded so kind, and so worried for me. Then he said, 'You'll get an OTP, just read it out so I can block it.' My finger was already on the message. And something in my head said, wait. Why would the bank need my OTP to protect me? So I said I'd call back. I hung up and called the number printed on the back of my card. The real bank said there was no problem at all. It was a scam. I was shaking after. Anyone can be fooled, didi. Never share the OTP."

qa.q: How many digits of Harish's card did the caller know?
How did Harish feel during and after the call?
qa.a: Harish felt trusting at first because the caller sounded kind and worried, then shaken after realising it was a scam.

qa.q: What did Harish do that protected the account?
qa.a: Harish refused to share the OTP, hung up, and called the official number printed on the back of the card to verify.

qa.q: How might Usha-didi feel hearing this story?
qa.a: She may feel alarmed but grateful, and more alert to similar calls herself.

grounding: A caller posing as the bank sounds friendly and urgent; the protagonist refuses to share the OTP and verifies through the official number.

passage:
Monday: Kalyani got a call from a "recruiter" named Priya offering a data-entry job at a big company, work from home, good pay. "You're shortlisted! Just pay a small registration fee today for the training kit." Kalyani felt a thrill. She'd been job-hunting for months.
Tuesday: The recruiter called twice, sounding friendly but more urgent. "Other candidates are waiting." Kalyani mentioned it to her friend Aadhya, who frowned. "Real companies don't charge you to get a job."
Wednesday: Kalyani looked up the company's official careers page. There was a warning in bold: "We never ask candidates for fees. Beware of fake recruiters." Her face went hot. She had almost paid.
Thursday: When the recruiter called again, Kalyani said, "I've checked with the company. I won't be paying anything." The line went dead. She reported the number on the national cybercrime portal, and told her cousins so they'd know too.

qa.q: What did the recruiter ask Kalyani to pay?
qa.a: A small registration fee for the training kit.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she saw the company's warning?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and shaken, her face hot, realising she had almost paid a scammer.
She verified through the company's official careers page, refused to pay any fee, reported the number, and warned her cousins.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see the recruiter's offer?
qa.a: Aadhya sees the fee as a red flag and is concerned for Kalyani, which is why she speaks up.

grounding: A friendly, urgent fake recruiter asks for an upfront fee; the protagonist verifies through official channels, refuses to pay and reports it.
